claims.text: Increasing atomic-size mismatch in a single-phase HEA increases lattice distortion.
Enhanced lattice distortion impedes dislocation movement.
Increasing lattice distortion produces higher hardness and strength than a low-mismatch baseline.
An equimolar solid solution made from elements with similar atomic radii has minimal lattice distortion.
Using constituents with similar atomic radii ensures a uniform microstructure.
Incremental substitution by an element with a more dissimilar atomic radius will systematically increase the lattice-distortion parameter.
XRD peak broadening and pair-distribution-function analysis can quantify the degree of lattice distortion.
Lattice distortion reflects local variations in interatomic distances.
Enhanced lattice distortion creates stronger local stress fields.
Distortion-induced local stress fields hinder dislocation glide.
The resulting solid-solution strengthening increases resistance to plastic deformation and thereby raises hardness and yield strength.
Modified HEAs with greater mismatch will show statistically significant increases in nanoindentation hardness and tensile yield strength relative to the baseline.
Secondary-phase precipitation can provide a strengthening contribution independent of the proposed single-phase lattice-distortion mechanism.
Local chemical complexity and processing variations may change the quantitative relationship between lattice distortion, hardness, and strength.
Excessive solute substitution may trigger phase decomposition.
Phase decomposition or precipitate formation would complicate attributing strength and hardness changes solely to lattice distortion.

contradictions.description: The boundary states that the hypothesis applies only while the alloy remains a single-phase solid solution, but the falsification rule treats observation of phase decomposition or precipitation as falsification. Such an observation instead places the specimen outside the stated applicability domain and confounds the proposed mechanism.
